title: Software Testing in Practice
subtitle: From a production horror story to a working testing strategy: test types, TDD, coverage, CI gating, and progressive delivery techniques.
contentMarkdown:
## Software Testing in Practice

### 1. Why Bother? A Case Study

**The scenario:** an HR Portal was developed on a low-code/customisable platform (SharePoint), with a customisable data structure and workflows. It had no local development environment, extremely slow deployment, painful release cycles, and unhappy users.

**Why it got so bad:**
- Issues were only caught in production — never earlier.
- Business logic was heavily coupled to the platform, making it hard to isolate and change safely.
- The development environment was extremely inefficient (no fast local loop).
- It was hard to work as a team — changes collided.
- There was a **negative compounding effect**: each new problem made the next change riskier and slower.

**Lessons:**
- Your reputation is affected by the quality of the software you release.
- The hard part of software engineering isn't writing the first version — it's **ensuring software keeps working correctly as it changes over time.**
- More automated tests would have caught this earlier.

**How automated tests would have helped:**
- Issues get caught early in the development process, not in production.
- Writing tests **forces you to abstract out external dependencies and isolate logic** (untestable code is usually a sign of tangled coupling).
- Testing changes in a local development environment is much faster than testing in production.
- Tests catch when one team member's changes interfere with and break another's code.
- Testing has a **positive compounding effect** — the inverse of the horror story's negative one: good tests make each subsequent change safer and faster, not riskier and slower.

### 2. Testing Attitude

- Your attitude towards testing determines its value.
- Good tests lead to **acceleration**, not overhead — a test suite is a fast feedback mechanism.
- It helps you refactor and abstract dependencies in your code correctly.
- It makes sure a growing codebase remains maintainable.
- **Tests should not be an afterthought — they are development,** not something bolted on after "the real work" is done.

### 3. Testing Concepts (the test types)

- **Unit** — does this one piece of logic do what it claims?
- **Integration** — do these pieces work together?
- **Functional** — does this feature behave as intended?
- **E2E (End-to-End)** — does the whole journey work, from the user's perspective?
- **Load** — does it hold up when the users show up (i.e. under realistic/peak traffic)?

### 4. Implementing Tests

- Design code to be **testable** — testability is a design property, not something you retrofit for free.
- **Name tests appropriately** — the name should immediately tell you what failed, without needing to read the test body.
- Tests can serve as **self-documentation** of a system's intended behaviour — a well-named, well-written test tells a future reader what the code is supposed to do.

### 5. Code Coverage

- Code coverage is a metric showing **how much of your code is being exercised by tests.**
- Tooling can show which lines of code are executed, and which branches are traversed, by the test suite.
- An open question for any team: **what percentage of code must be covered** before a change is considered adequately tested? (There's no universal number — coverage is a signal, not a guarantee of correctness; 100% coverage does not mean zero bugs, and low coverage on critical logic is a red flag regardless of the overall percentage.)

### 6. Test-Driven Development (TDD) — Red, Green, Refactor

1. **Red** — write the test(s) first. They will fail, since the implementation doesn't exist yet.
2. **Green** — implement just enough code to make the failing tests pass.
3. **Refactor** — clean up the code (and/or the tests) now that you have passing tests as a safety net.

A key benefit: **TDD eliminates premature optimisation** — you write the simplest code that satisfies the test, then improve it, rather than trying to design the "perfect" implementation upfront before you even know it behaves correctly.

### 7. Testing Strategy

**Continuous Integration:**
- Tests should run on **every** code change.
- Pull requests cannot succeed (cannot be merged) unless tests have passed.
- This ensures teams can collaborate and deliver quality together — a shared, enforced quality gate rather than an individual discipline.

**User Acceptance Testing (UAT):**
- Not all testing can be automated — some features genuinely require human verification.
- Humans can break things in unexpected ways. A really good manual tester is an extremely valuable team member, precisely because they find the paths automated tests didn't anticipate.
- It's far better to catch an unexpected end-user action during testing than in production.

### 8. Testing Strategy — Advanced

- **Smoke tests** — a limited set of tests covering critical paths, used to quickly verify a deployment succeeded (i.e. "did the basic things not catastrophically break").
- **Feature switches / dark features (feature flags)** — ship code to production without exposing it to users yet. This **decouples deployment from release** — the code can be deployed and verified safely, then "released" (turned on) independently, and rolled back instantly by flipping the flag rather than re-deploying.
- **Canary releases** — roll a change out to a small subset of users/traffic first, to reduce risk and/or measure user reaction, before a full rollout.

### 9. Key Takeaways

- **Plan for testing** — have an explicit testing strategy, don't leave it implicit.
- **Design for testability** — testable code is a design outcome, not an accident.
- **Automated tests have a compounding effect** — good tests make future change safer and faster; poor/absent tests make future change riskier and slower (the horror story's negative compounding effect, inverted).
- **Implement against tests** — write the test first (or alongside), and execute tests consistently (e.g. via CI on every change), not sporadically.

mcqs.q: In the HR Portal case study, what was identified as a primary reason issues went undetected until it was too late?
options: The team used too many automated tests
Issues were only caught in production
The platform had too much unit test coverage
The team over-invested in TDD
mcqs.explanation: "Only caught issues in production" is listed first among the reasons the HR Portal situation got so bad.

mcqs.q: Why does writing tests force you to "abstract out external dependencies and isolate logic"?
options: Testing frameworks require all code to be written in a functional style
Code tightly coupled to external dependencies (e.g. a specific platform) is hard to test in isolation, so testability pressures you toward decoupling
Unit tests automatically mock the database for you
Integration tests replace the need for abstraction entirely
mcqs.explanation: The HR Portal's business logic was "heavily coupled to the platform" — writing tests for coupled code is painful, which pushes developers toward isolating logic from its dependencies.

mcqs.q: What is the "negative compounding effect" described in the case study?
options: Automated tests becoming slower with every release
Each new problem in an untested, coupled codebase makes the next change riskier and slower, compounding over time
Code coverage percentage decreasing with every release
The number of engineers needed doubling every year
mcqs.explanation: The lecture lists a "negative compounding effect" as a reason the HR Portal situation deteriorated, contrasted later with testing's positive compounding effect.

mcqs.q: According to the "Testing Attitude" section, what should a good test suite function as?
options: A compliance checkbox required before release
A fast feedback mechanism that leads to acceleration instead of overhead
A replacement for code review
An optional step performed only before major releases
mcqs.explanation: "A test suite is a fast feedback mechanism" and "good tests lead to acceleration instead of overhead" are stated directly.

mcqs.q: Which test type answers the question "does this one piece of logic do what it claims?"
options: Integration
Unit
E2E
Load
mcqs.explanation: Unit tests target one isolated piece of logic.

mcqs.q: Which test type answers "does the whole journey work, from the user's perspective?"
options: Unit
Functional
E2E
Integration
mcqs.explanation: End-to-end (E2E) tests verify the full user journey, not an isolated piece or pairing of components.

mcqs.q: Which test type specifically answers "do these pieces work together?"
options: Unit
Integration
Load
E2E
mcqs.explanation: Integration tests verify that multiple pieces/components function correctly together.

mcqs.q: What does Load testing primarily verify?
options: Whether individual functions return correct values
Whether the system holds up when users actually show up (realistic/peak traffic)
Whether a feature behaves as intended for a single user
Whether two components work together correctly
mcqs.explanation: Load testing answers "does it hold up when the users show up?" — a question about capacity/performance under real traffic, not correctness of a single function or feature.

mcqs.q: Why does the lecture emphasize naming tests so "the name should immediately tell you what failed"?
options: So test names can double as documentation and let a reader diagnose a failure without reading the test body
Because test frameworks require alphabetically sorted test names
Because CI pipelines fail if test names exceed a character limit
Because coverage tools cannot process ambiguous test names
mcqs.explanation: The lecture states tests "can serve as self-documentation of the behaviour of a system" — a clear name is central to that.

mcqs.q: What is code coverage a metric of?
options: How many bugs exist in the codebase
How much of the code is executed by the test suite (lines/branches)
How many developers contributed to a file
How fast the test suite runs
mcqs.explanation: Coverage tooling shows which lines and branches were executed by the tests — not correctness or bug count directly.

mcqs.q: Which statement about code coverage best reflects the lecture's framing?
options: 100% code coverage guarantees zero bugs
The required coverage percentage is left as an open question for teams, and coverage is a signal rather than a guarantee of correctness
Coverage should never be measured, as it discourages testing
Only integration tests count toward code coverage
mcqs.explanation: The lecture poses "what percentage of code must be covered?" as an open question rather than asserting a fixed number or claiming coverage proves correctness.

mcqs.q: In TDD's Red-Green-Refactor cycle, what happens during "Red"?
options: Code is refactored for performance
Tests are written first and are expected to fail, since the implementation doesn't exist yet
All existing tests are deleted
The application is deployed to production
mcqs.explanation: "Write the tests first, which will fail" is the Red phase — no implementation exists yet to make them pass.

mcqs.q: What is one stated benefit of TDD regarding code design decisions?
options: It guarantees the fastest possible runtime performance
It eliminates premature optimisation, since you write the simplest code to pass the test before improving it
It removes the need for code review
It requires exactly 100% code coverage by definition
mcqs.explanation: The lecture states TDD "eliminates premature optimisation" — you implement just enough to pass, then refactor.

mcqs.q: Under a CI-based testing strategy, what must be true before a pull request can be merged?
options: A manual UAT tester must approve it, regardless of automated results
Tests must run and pass — the PR cannot succeed unless tests have passed
Code coverage must reach exactly 100%
The PR must include a canary release plan
mcqs.explanation: "Pull Requests cannot succeed unless tests have passed" is stated directly under the Continuous Integration strategy.

mcqs.q: Why does the lecture argue a good manual/UAT tester is extremely valuable, even with strong automated coverage?
options: Manual testers replace the need for CI entirely
Not all testing can be automated, and humans can break things in unexpected ways automated tests didn't anticipate
Manual testers are required to write all future automated tests
UAT is only useful for load testing
mcqs.explanation: "Not all testing can be automated... humans can break things in unexpected ways" is given as the reason a good tester is valuable.

mcqs.q: What is the primary purpose of a smoke test?
options: To achieve 100% code coverage on critical paths
To quickly verify limited critical paths still work, confirming a deployment didn't catastrophically break something
To replace unit tests for core business logic
To simulate thousands of concurrent users
mcqs.explanation: Smoke tests "verify limited critical paths to verify a deployment" — a fast, shallow sanity check, not exhaustive coverage.

mcqs.q: What do feature switches (dark features) allow a team to do?
options: Permanently disable a feature after release
Ship code to production without exposing it to users yet, decoupling deployment from release
Automatically generate unit tests for new features
Bypass CI checks for urgent hotfixes
mcqs.explanation: Feature flags let you deploy code dark and "decouple deployment from release" — deploying and releasing become two separate, independently-controlled actions.

mcqs.q: What is a canary release used for?
options: Rolling a change out to a small subset of users/traffic first, to reduce risk or measure reaction before a full rollout
Running tests exclusively in an isolated branch that never merges
Replacing smoke tests entirely
Testing database migrations only
mcqs.explanation: Canary releases are explicitly described as being "used to reduce risk or test user reaction" via a limited initial rollout.

mcqs.q: How do feature flags and canary releases differ in what they primarily control?
options: Feature flags control code visibility to users; canary releases control what portion of traffic/users receives a change
They are functionally identical techniques with different names
Feature flags require production deployment; canary releases do not
Canary releases only apply to database schema changes
mcqs.explanation: A feature flag toggles whether a shipped feature is visible at all; a canary release controls how much traffic/how many users see a given version — related but distinct levers.

mcqs.q: Which statement best captures the lecture's core argument about testing and reputation/velocity?
options: Testing is purely a quality-assurance formality with no effect on delivery speed
Good automated testing has a compounding effect that accelerates future development and protects reputation, while untested, coupled code compounds negatively and slows teams down
Manual testing is strictly superior to automated testing for velocity
Testing should only begin once a product is close to release
mcqs.explanation: This is the throughline of the whole lecture: the HR Portal's negative compounding effect versus testing's positive compounding effect, and "your reputation is affected by the quality of the software you release."

techQuestions.q: Using the HR Portal case study, trace the causal chain from "no local development environment" to "users were very unhappy," and identify which single automated testing practice would have broken that chain earliest.
techQuestions.answer:
**The causal chain:** no local development environment → developers can't quickly verify a change works before committing it → issues are only discovered once code reaches production → each production issue has to be diagnosed and fixed under pressure, on a platform where business logic is heavily coupled to the platform itself → fixes are slow and risky because there's no fast, isolated way to test a fix before shipping it → release cycles become painful and slow → users experience frequent breakage and slow turnaround on fixes → users are unhappy. This is the "negative compounding effect" the lecture names directly: each step makes the next step worse.

**Where the chain could have been broken earliest:** a fast local **unit/integration test suite** that developers run *before* committing would have caught logic errors before they ever reached the shared, slow-to-deploy production-like environment. This is earlier in the chain than CI (which still requires a push), earlier than smoke tests (which run post-deployment), and earlier than UAT (which happens even later). The lecture's own answer to "how would automated tests have helped" leads with exactly this: "we would've caught issues early on in the development process" and "testing changes in the development environment would've been much faster" — i.e. a fast local test loop is the earliest possible intervention point in this specific chain.

techQuestions.q: Explain the difference between "code coverage" as a metric and "test quality." Why can a codebase have high coverage but still ship serious bugs?

Design a test-pyramid-style plan (unit / integration / functional / E2E / load) for a feature: "users can upload a profile photo, which is resized and stored in cloud storage." Give one concrete example test case for each level.
techQuestions.answer:
- **Unit** — isolate the pure logic with no I/O. Example: `resizeImage(buffer, targetWidth)` given a known input image buffer, returns a buffer whose decoded dimensions match `targetWidth` (mocking/stubbing out any actual filesystem or network calls).
- **Integration** — verify the pieces work together, using real-but-local dependencies where practical. Example: the `PhotoUploadService.upload()` method, given a raw image buffer, correctly calls the resize function *and* writes the resulting bytes to a real (test/ephemeral) storage bucket, then reads it back and confirms the stored bytes match — proving the resize step and the storage client integrate correctly.
- **Functional** — verify the feature behaves as intended from an API/feature-level perspective. Example: `POST /users/:id/profile-photo` with a valid JPEG returns `200` and a URL; fetching that URL returns an image with the expected resized dimensions and content-type.
- **E2E** — verify the whole journey from the user's perspective, through the real UI. Example: a browser-driven test that logs in as a user, navigates to profile settings, selects a photo file via the file picker, clicks "upload," and asserts the new photo visibly appears as the profile picture on the page.
- **Load** — verify the system holds up under realistic traffic. Example: simulate 200 concurrent users uploading photos within a 60-second window and assert the 95th-percentile response time stays under an agreed threshold (e.g. 2 seconds) with no failed uploads.

techQuestions.q: Explain the Red-Green-Refactor cycle using a concrete example: implementing `calculateShippingCost(weight, distance)`. Walk through what happens at each phase.
A team says: "We don't need CI-enforced tests — our developers are disciplined enough to run tests locally before pushing." Critique this position using the lecture's CI testing strategy points.
techQuestions.answer:
This position has several concrete weaknesses the lecture's CI strategy directly addresses:

1. **It relies on discipline, not enforcement.** The lecture's CI point is explicit: "Pull Requests cannot succeed unless tests have passed" — a hard gate, not a request. Human discipline is inconsistent under deadline pressure ("I'll just push this one small fix, I already tested it locally, mostly") — exactly the scenario CI exists to remove reliance on.
2. **It doesn't scale with team size.** "This ensures that teams can collaborate and deliver quality together" — with one disciplined developer, self-enforcement might mostly work; with a growing team, the probability that *someone*, *sometime*, skips the local run approaches certainty, and there's no shared, auditable record that tests actually ran and passed for every change.
3. **"Ran locally" and "ran against what's actually being merged" can diverge.** A developer's local branch may not include the latest changes from `main` that just landed from someone else — a locally-green test run doesn't prove the *merged result* is green. CI running tests against the actual merge target closes this gap.
4. **No visible, shared signal for reviewers.** A reviewer approving a PR has no reliable way to know "yes, tests were run and passed" without CI providing that status directly on the PR — trusting a verbal/implicit claim isn't the same as an enforced, visible check.

The underlying principle from the lecture is that testing should be a **team-level guarantee**, not an individual one — CI enforcement is what converts "our developers are disciplined" (a hope) into "our pull requests cannot merge without passing tests" (a guarantee).

techQuestions.q: The lecture states "tests should not be an afterthought — they are development." What does this imply about *when* in the development process tests should be written, and how does it relate to designing code to be testable?
techQuestions.answer:
Treating tests as an afterthought means writing the implementation first, then trying to bolt tests onto it once it's "done." The lecture's framing rejects that ordering: tests are not a separate QA phase performed *after* development, they *are* part of the act of developing the feature — writing the test and writing the implementation are the same activity, not sequential ones (the extreme version of this is literally TDD's Red-Green-Refactor, where the test is written *before* any implementation exists at all).

**Why this matters for testability:** if tests are written only after the implementation is finished, the implementation was designed with zero pressure to be testable — it's easy to end up with code tightly coupled to specific external dependencies (a database client, the system clock, a third-party API) because nothing forced the developer to think about how those dependencies would be isolated during testing. This is precisely the HR Portal's failure mode: "business logic was heavily coupled to the platform," making it hard to test in isolation after the fact.

Writing tests *as part of* development — ideally before or alongside the implementation — forces early decisions like "this function needs its dependencies injected rather than hardcoded" or "this piece of logic should be a pure function separate from its I/O," *while the code is still being shaped*, rather than trying to retrofit those boundaries onto already-tangled code later. Testability becomes a natural consequence of treating testing as development, not an afterthought bolted on once the design is already locked in.

techQuestions.q: Compare feature flags (dark features) and canary releases: describe one scenario where you'd use only a feature flag, one where you'd use only a canary release, and one where you'd combine both.
techQuestions.answer:
**Feature flag only:** a new "export to PDF" button is fully built and deployed to production, but it's not ready for any users to see yet — perhaps the design team wants to demo it internally first, or the launch needs to be coordinated with a marketing announcement date. The code ships to production behind a flag that's off for everyone; when the announcement date arrives, the team flips the flag on for all users simultaneously, with zero additional deployment needed. Here you don't need a *gradual* rollout — you need a *deployment/release timing* decoupling, which a flag alone provides.

**Canary release only:** a team rewrites the checkout service's internal payment-processing logic — the change isn't a new visible feature (there's nothing to "hide" behind a flag; the button and flow look identical to users), but it's high-risk because it touches money movement. Routing 5% of production checkout traffic through the new version first, while the rest continues on the old version, lets the team compare error rates and payment-success rates before trusting it with 100% of traffic. Here there's no user-facing toggle needed — you need a *risk-limiting, gradually-increasing exposure* mechanism, which canarying provides.

**Combined:** a major redesign of the onboarding flow is both risky (new code path, could have bugs) and something the team wants to validate gradually with real user reaction, not just error rates. The new flow ships behind a feature flag (decoupling deploy from release — the code can sit in production, verified via smoke tests, without any user seeing it), and when it's time to test it live, the flag is enabled only for a canary segment of users (e.g. 10%) so the team can measure both technical health (errors, latency) *and* product signals (completion rate, drop-off) before progressively increasing the percentage to 100%. The flag controls *whether* the new logic can be reached at all; the canary percentage controls *how much* traffic reaches it at any given point — using both together gives the team fine-grained control over both dimensions.

techQuestions.q: A developer argues automated tests are "overhead that slows down delivery." Using the lecture's compounding effect argument, construct a counter-argument grounded in a specific 6-month example.
techQuestions.answer:
**The developer's framing treats testing as a fixed, one-time cost** — time spent writing tests instead of writing features. The lecture's compounding effect argument says this misses the *time-dependent* nature of the trade-off: the cost/benefit of testing isn't constant, it compounds in opposite directions over time depending on whether you invest in it or not.

**Concrete 6-month example — Team A (no tests) vs. Team B (invests in tests), same feature set:**

- **Month 1:** Team A ships features slightly faster — no time spent writing tests. Team B ships slightly slower, having written unit and integration tests alongside each feature.
- **Month 2–3:** Team A starts touching earlier code to add new features. Because nothing verifies existing behaviour, each change risks silently breaking something built in month 1 — bugs surface days or weeks later, often in production, and take time to trace back to their real cause (exactly the "only caught issues in production" failure mode from the HR Portal case study). Team B's tests catch regressions in *seconds*, locally, before the change is even pushed — refactoring and extending old code is low-risk because the safety net is already there.
- **Month 4–6:** Team A's velocity is now visibly *decreasing* — every new feature requires manual regression-testing of unrelated areas "just in case," release cycles slow down, and trust in the software erodes (matching "your reputation is affected by the quality of the software you release"). Team B's velocity holds steady or increases — new features build confidently on a codebase whose existing behaviour is continuously verified, and the test suite itself increasingly documents how the system is supposed to work, reducing onboarding/context-switching cost.

**The counter-argument, stated directly:** testing isn't overhead subtracted once from month 1's velocity — it's an investment that inverts the sign of a compounding effect. Skipping it doesn't remove a cost, it defers and *compounds* it as accumulating regression risk, debugging time, and slowed releases across every subsequent month — which is a strictly worse trade over any timeline longer than a few weeks.

techQuestions.q: Explain what "testability" means as a code design property, and give a concrete before/after example of code refactored to be more testable by isolating a hard dependency (e.g. the current time).
Why does the lecture insist that "not all testing can be automated"? Give two categories of issues a good manual/UAT tester would catch that automated tests structurally cannot.
techQuestions.answer:
Automated tests can only check what they were explicitly written to check — they execute a predetermined script and compare the result against a predetermined expectation. They have no capacity for judgment, curiosity, or improvisation; a human tester does, and the lecture points to this directly: "humans can break things in unexpected ways" — precisely the class of problem a fixed, pre-written test script cannot cover by definition, because if a team anticipated the exact failure mode, they would already have written an automated test for it. It is *unanticipated* usage that requires a human.

**Two categories a human catches that automated tests structurally cannot:**

1. **Subjective UX/usability judgment.** An automated test can assert that a button exists, is clickable, and triggers the correct API call — it cannot assess whether the resulting flow is *confusing*, whether error messages are *helpful* in context, or whether a layout *feels* cluttered on an actual device. This requires human perception and judgment about the experience, not verification of a discrete, specifiable outcome.

2. **Unanticipated real-world usage patterns.** A human tester might, without being told to, try pasting an emoji into a numeric field, double-clicking "submit" rapidly, using the browser's back button mid-checkout, or resizing the window mid-upload — none of which anyone thought to write an automated test for, precisely because no one anticipated a user would do it. Automated tests only cover paths someone already imagined; a curious human tester actively searches for paths *nobody* imagined, which is exactly the "unexpected end-user action" the lecture says is better caught in testing than in production.

techQuestions.q: Explain the relationship between smoke tests and the rest of the automated test suite in a deployment pipeline. Why not just rely on the full test suite that already passed in CI before deployment?
techQuestions.answer:
The full CI test suite (unit, integration, functional, E2E) verifies that the **code itself** is correct, typically run against a build artifact in a CI runner or staging-like environment *before* deployment. A smoke test runs **after** a specific deployment, against the **actual freshly-deployed environment**, and checks a small set of critical paths to confirm the deployment itself succeeded — a fundamentally different concern from code correctness.

**Why the pre-deploy test suite passing isn't sufficient on its own:** CI proves the code is correct in the environment CI ran it in — it says nothing about whether *this specific deployment*, to *this specific environment*, actually came up correctly. Things that can go wrong purely at deployment time, which a pre-deploy test suite structurally cannot catch, include:
- A missing or misconfigured environment variable/secret in the target environment
- A database migration that didn't actually run, or ran against the wrong database
- A networking/DNS/load-balancer misconfiguration preventing the new instances from receiving traffic
- The wrong container image or build artifact actually being deployed
- A dependency (e.g. an external API, a cache, a message broker) being unreachable from the new environment specifically

A smoke test is a fast, narrow, post-deployment sanity check that answers "did the thing that just got deployed actually come up and serve the critical paths correctly in this real environment?" — a question the earlier, code-focused test suite is not positioned to answer, since it never actually touches the real deployment target. This is why the lecture lists smoke tests as a distinct, additional layer of the testing strategy rather than treating a passing CI run as sufficient on its own.
